tx.t: This lecture looks at the history and the future of electric cars. Electric vehicles are older than many people think. The first ones appeared in the eighteen thirties.
Around the year nineteen hundred, more than a quarter of the cars on American roads were electric. Petrol cars then became cheaper and could travel further, so electric cars almost disappeared.

Modern electric cars use lithium-ion batteries, which store more energy for their weight. Their main advantage is that they produce no exhaust gases while driving, though making the batteries does cause pollution.

tx.t: In this talk I would like to tell the story of chocolate. Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which first grew in Central and South America.

The Maya and the Aztecs drank a bitter chocolate drink, often with chilli, and sometimes used the beans as money. Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, and people began to add sugar.
The first solid eating chocolate was made by an English company, Fry, in eighteen forty-seven. Milk chocolate was invented by a Swiss man, Daniel Peter, in eighteen seventy-five.

In nineteen oh three she won the Nobel Prize in Physics, becoming the first woman ever to win a Nobel Prize. In nineteen eleven she won a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry.
During the First World War, she developed mobile X-ray units that doctors used to treat wounded soldiers. She died in nineteen thirty-four, probably because of her long exposure to radiation.

The students who used the method of testing themselves instead of rereading scored higher in the final exam. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.

tx.t: Let me tell you something about the history and the economics of coffee. According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia by a goat herder called Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became lively after eating the berries.

By the fifteenth century, coffee was grown in Yemen, and it then spread to Turkey and Europe. There are two main kinds of coffee, Arabica and Robusta, and about sixty per cent of the world's coffee is Arabica.
Brazil produces about one third of the world's coffee, more than any other country. People around the world drink about two billion cups of coffee every day.

tx.t: In this lecture we will look at the diversity of languages around the world. About forty per cent of them are endangered, which means they are at risk of disappearing.

Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, while English is the most widely spoken language overall. Papua New Guinea is the most linguistically diverse country, with more than eight hundred languages.
Just twenty-three languages account for more than half of the world's population. A language usually disappears when children stop learning it at home.
